strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: low-bit (W4A4/W4A3) quantization of diffusion models, where activation outliers and their accumulation across denoising steps cause severe degradation.

The core technical observation is sound and practically relevant: applying the Hadamard rotation only to activations (Single Hadamard Transformation) keeps the offline-transformed weight matrix outlier-free and makes integer convolution feasible, whereas rotating weights offline (Double Hadamard Transformation) can amplify weight outliers and is incompatible with strided convolutions. Equations (13)-(18) correctly exploit orthogonality to fold the rotation into integer arithmetic with scales absorbing the 2^{-k/2} factor.

Empirical results are competitive: consistent improvements over EfficientDM at W4A4 and dramatic gains at W4A3 on ImageNet 256x256 (IS 49.62 vs 8.74), plus gains on LSUN-Bedrooms and LSUN-Churches, achieved with hardware-friendlier symmetric activation quantization.
The paper includes an ablation on the Hadamard block order and visualization evidence (channel-wise max-abs before/after transformation) supporting the outlier-reduction motivation.

The distillation design (LoRA fine-tuning + timestep-wise learnable scales) is sensibly composed from established components (EfficientDM, LSQ), and the convergence comparison in Figure 4 suggests more stable training at very low activation bits.
weaknesses: Limited novelty with overclaiming: the paper claims to propose 'for the first time' the Single Hadamard Transformation, but applying a rotation to activations only (keeping weights unrotated) is a straightforward consequence of inserting identity HH^T, and activation-only rotations are common in the rotation-based quantization literature (QuaRot, SpinQuant-style methods, I-BERT/Int8 line of work). The effective contribution is an adaptation of QuaRot-style rotations into the EfficientDM QAT distillation pipeline, which is incremental.

The central 'hardware-friendly' claim is never validated empirically: there are no latency, throughput, memory, or bit-OP measurements, no comparison of the added on-the-fly Hadamard multiplication cost against simply rotating weights offline, and no actual integer-only implementation benchmark. For a paper whose key selling point is hardware efficiency, this is a significant evidentiary gap.

Results are mixed and the presentation cherry-picks metrics: at W8A4 on ImageNet, HQ-DM's FID (7.68) is worse than EfficientDM (6.75); the headline '467.73% IS improvement' at W4A3 is measured against a completely collapsed baseline (IS 8.74), which inflates the apparent gain. The abstract and intro emphasize IS gains while underplaying FID regressions.

Several inconsistencies and presentation problems undermine confidence: Table 2's text-reported FID reductions (e.g., '3.49' for W3A4) do not match the table (20.92->19.22 = 1.70); references are duplicated (TFMQ-DM appears as [23] and [24], LSQ as [12] and [13]); typos such as 'Xi at al.'; the claim of 'data-free fine-tuning' is stated but the setup and whether any real or generated calibration data is used is never clearly specified.

The appendix (Section 7) contains only visualizations despite the text repeatedly referring to 'the Appendix' for experimental details. Training hyperparameters, computational cost, number of trainable parameters, LoRA rank, and reproducibility details are missing; no code release is mentioned.

The convolution treatment is under-justified: applying the Hadamard transform along the spatial width dimension of the activation tensor (rather than channels, as in standard rotation-based methods) is unusual and the paper provides little analysis of why this specific axis choice is effective or how it interacts with padding/strides.

The ablation over Hadamard orders (k=3..6) shows differences well within likely noise (e.g., IS 245.11-249.24), yet the paper concludes a specific optimum (k=5); no variance or repeated-run statistics are reported anywhere.

Generality is overclaimed: experiments cover only LDM-4/LDM-8 on class-conditional and unconditional generation; no text-to-image (e.g., Stable Diffusion) or latent video model is evaluated, yet the paper claims 'strong generalization potential for diffusion model quantization.'

Some of the outlier visualizations (Figures 5-10 in the appendix) show post-transformation peaks that are sometimes higher than pre-transformation, weakening the qualitative outlier-suppression narrative the main figure implies.

strengths: The paper targets a practically relevant problem (activation outliers in low-bit quantization of diffusion models) and shows consistent empirical gains over EfficientDM and other baselines in aggressive low-bit settings (W4A3, W3A4) across three datasets (ImageNet 256x256, LSUN-Bedrooms, LSUN-Churches).

The motivation for applying the Hadamard rotation only to activations (avoiding outlier amplification when rotating already well-behaved weight matrices, and supporting integer convolution) is intuitively reasonable and supported by the channel-wise outlier visualizations in Figures 2 and 3(c).
The framework is relatively simple and composable (rotation + LoRA distillation + timestep-wise learned scales), which could make adoption easy if the technical details were fully specified.
An ablation on the Hadamard matrix order (Table 4) and training convergence curves (Figure 4) are provided, and comparisons cover multiple PTQ and QAT baselines.
weaknesses: The central novelty claim is overclaimed. Applying a Hadamard/orthogonal rotation to activations only (while leaving weights unrotated) is essentially the 'online rotation' strategy already used in QuaRot and related LLM quantization work, and the LoRA-based distillation pipeline is directly adopted from EfficientDM, with timestep-wise scales adopted from LSQ. The framing 'we propose, for the first time, the Single Hadamard Transformation' is not accurate; the actual delta over prior work is a repositioning of an existing technique into diffusion-model QAT, which is an incremental contribution.

The technical soundness of the convolution case (Eqs. 16-18) is not convincingly established. Applying a block-diagonal Hadamard matrix along the reshaped width dimension and then asserting integer convolution equivalence requires the transform to commute with the convolution operation; since the rotation acts on the spatial (width) axis that the kernel itself convolves over, the claimed factorization Conv((X~c Hc)_int · Hc, Wc_int) into pure integer arithmetic appears questionable (unlike the channel-dimension case for linear layers, where orthogonality genuinely permits the identity insertion). No derivation, proof, or per-layer numerical equivalence check is provided to dispel this concern.

Despite repeated claims of being 'hardware-friendly' and supporting 'INT convolution', the paper reports no actual hardware measurements: no latency, throughput, memory, or kernel-level benchmarks. The efficiency claims rest entirely on theoretical argument, and since the integer pipeline apparently requires an extra Hadamard multiplication (and its inverse) per layer plus dequantization, the real speedup relative to EfficientDM is unverified.

The headline quantitative claims are selectively favorable. The abstract and text emphasize IS gains (+12.8%, +467.73%), but under several settings HQ-DM is worse on key metrics (e.g., W8A4 FID 7.68 vs. EfficientDM's 6.75 on ImageNet; IS 248.30 vs. QuEST's 5.98 FID at W4A4), and no variance or significance testing is reported. The 467.73% figure is inflated relative to a near-collapsed baseline.

Reproducibility is weak. The text repeatedly defers to an 'Appendix' for implementation details, but the submission contains no appendix with hyperparameters, training schedules, or architecture-specific handling details; Section 7 ('Additional Visualization Results') appears after the conclusion as a stub. No code release is mentioned, and several references are broken or duplicated (TFMQ-DM cited as [23] and [24]; LSQ as [12] and [13]; 'Anonymous' and 'B. Li et al.' entries), suggesting rushed preparation.

The ablation on Hadamard order (Table 4) does not support the conclusion drawn: differences between k=3, 5, and 6 are within noise (IS 249.24 vs. 248.30 vs. 249.04), and the stated claim that k=5 is optimal is not statistically substantiated.

Evaluation is limited to small LDM-4/LDM-8 models with class-conditional or unconditional generation; no experiments on text-to-image models (e.g., Stable Diffusion), which is where outlier-driven quantization difficulty and the practical relevance of this line of work are strongest. There is also no discussion of limitations or societal impact.

Some method descriptions are internally inconsistent or confusing, e.g., claiming the scheme enables operations 'without requiring subsequent dequantization' while Eqs. 13 and 16 explicitly include a dequantization step, and the 'Single vs. Double Hadamard' terminology is not rigorously defined relative to prior literature.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: activation outliers that prevent low-bit quantization of diffusion models, and the core technical idea (applying the Hadamard rotation to activations only, with the 2^{-k/2} normalization factor absorbed into floating-point scales) is sound and cleanly derived. The derivation of integer-only matrix multiplication (Eqs. 13-18) and the convolution variant (reshape + block-diagonal Hadamard along the width dimension) are clearly presented.

Empirical results are extensive and largely convincing: LDM-4 on ImageNet 256x256, LDM-4/8 on LSUN-Bedrooms and LSUN-Churches, across W8A8 through W4A3 settings, with consistent gains over EfficientDM and other baselines, particularly at very low activation bit-widths (W4A3), where the improvements are dramatic.

The ablation study on the Hadamard block order (k = 3..6) and the convergence comparison against EfficientDM (Figure 4) add useful analysis, and the symmetric (rather than asymmetric) activation quantization makes the proposed scheme more deployable than the baselines it compares against.
The motivation via channel-wise outlier analysis before/after transformation (Figures 2, 5-10) directly supports the central hypothesis and strengthens the experimental narrative.
weaknesses: Novelty is overstated. The 'Single Hadamard Transformation' is essentially the well-known activation-only rotation used in prior rotation-based quantization work (QuaRot, Xi et al. I-Fix/4-bit transformer training); the paper's framing as 'pioneering' and 'first' is not accurate at the level claimed. The genuinely new elements are the adaptation of this rotation to the EfficientDM-style LoRA distillation QAT framework and its application to convolutional diffusion models, which is a solid but incremental contribution. The paper should honestly position itself relative to prior Hadamard/rotation-based quantization literature.

Numerical inconsistencies between the text and the tables undermine confidence. Section 5.2 claims FID reductions of 3.49 (W3A4) and 5.98 (W4A3) on LSUN-Bedrooms, but Table 2 shows 1.70 and 4.92 respectively. Such mismatches must be corrected; they raise concerns about the overall reliability of the reported numbers.

No actual hardware measurements. The central claim of a 'hardware-friendly', INT-convolution-supporting scheme is not backed by any latency, throughput, or memory measurements on real accelerators. Without such evidence, the practical advantage over Double Hadamard Transformation remains asserted rather than demonstrated.

Limited model and task scope: experiments cover only LDM-4/LDM-8 class-conditional and unconditional generation. No text-to-image (e.g., Stable Diffusion) or DiT-based results, which limits evidence of generalization to the diffusion models of greatest practical interest.

Some baseline comparisons are incomplete or missing (e.g., many '-' cells for Q-Diffusion/PTQD/TFMQ-DM; QuEST compared only partially), and in several configurations HQ-DM is worse on some metrics than EfficientDM (e.g., W8A4 FID 7.68 vs 6.75 on ImageNet), which the text does not acknowledge.

The convolution-specific claim that the Double Hadamard Transformation is fundamentally incompatible with strided convolution is argued only informally; a precise treatment (e.g., im2col-based equivalents or why the width-dimension rotation suffices) is missing.

Reproducibility is weak: the paper repeatedly defers details to an 'Appendix', but the submission contains only visualization results (Section 7) — no training hyperparameters, LoRA ranks, calibration data details, or compute budgets. This prevents reproduction of the results.

Presentation issues: duplicated TFMQ-DM references ([23]/[24]), an anonymous citation ([1]), inconsistent citation formatting, and the ablation table (Table 4) shows k=3 achieving higher IS than the claimed-optimal k=5, which the text does not discuss. There is no limitations or societal-impact discussion.

strengths: The paper is well motivated: it clearly identifies two concrete limitations of the conventional Double Hadamard Transformation for diffusion model quantization (incompatibility with integer convolution, and amplification of outliers when applied to already-smooth weight matrices), and proposes a targeted remedy (Single Hadamard Transformation applied to activations only).

Experimental evaluation is broad and reasonably thorough: LDM-4/LDM-8 and DiT-XL backbones on ImageNet 256/512 and two LSUN datasets, multiple bit-widths (down to W4A3 / 4/3 and even 2/4 for baselines), and multiple metrics (IS, FID, sFID, Precision, Recall), with consistent gains that grow as activation bit-width decreases.

The comparison against the Double Hadamard variant (Table 6) is informative: it isolates the core contribution, showing both accuracy and ~10% latency advantages, and includes latency/efficiency measurements and training-time comparisons (Fig. 5c).

The ablation study (Table 5) is well designed, disentangling LSQ, LoRA distillation, and the Hadamard transformation, and showing that the transformation is beneficial even without learnable scales or LoRA (Naive PTQ+Hada., LoRA+Hada.), which strengthens the claim that gains come from outlier suppression rather than the inherited EfficientDM machinery.
The method retains the training efficiency of EfficientDM (1.4 h vs 28 h for TFMQ-DM-style calibration), supporting the practical relevance of the contribution.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the framework is essentially EfficientDM (LoRA-based distillation + timestep-aware LSQ) with a Hadamard rotation on activations. Rotation-based outlier suppression is well established (QuaRot, Xi et al. 4-bit integer training, SmoothQuant); the contribution is an adaptation to diffusion models plus the single-vs-double design choice. This should be stated more explicitly.

Technical justification for the convolution scheme is weak. For conv layers the Hadamard matrix is applied along the spatial width dimension (Eq. 13-14), not along channels, yet outliers in diffusion models are known to be channel-wise. No theoretical or empirical analysis is provided showing that mixing spatial positions reduces activation outliers in conv layers, and effects of padding and stride>1 on the identity-insertion argument are not discussed. This part of the method appears ad hoc and under-analyzed.

Some reported numbers warrant scrutiny: the quantized W4A4 model achieves FID 6.58 vs. 11.22 for the full-precision model on ImageNet (also on LSUN-Bedrooms, HQ-DM 4/4 FID 13.15 vs FP 7.56 discrepancy direction differs), and headline claims like '467.73% improvement in IS' are inflated relative presentations of near-degenerate baselines (IS 8.74 -> 49.62). The paper should discuss why quantized FID can beat FP and temper the percentage claims.

Missing baselines/comparisons: no comparison to other rotation- or Hadamard-based diffusion quantization methods, and QuEST is compared only partially (single configuration, missing sFID/Precision). Recall is omitted from Table 1 and Table 4 despite being listed as an evaluation metric.

Clarity issues: Fig. 3 contains an unexplained panel '(c) Pre/Post-Hadamard Weights'; Fig. 1 caption calls the method a 'distillation framework' while the abstract calls it a QAT framework; the data-free claim in the introduction is not reconciled with the distillation setup (what data does the teacher/student share?). No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility.

No limitations or societal-impact discussion is provided, and no analysis is given of failure cases or of when the block-diagonal Hadamard construction (when C_i is not a multiple of the block size beyond the H=I fallback) affects performance.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and relevant problem: activation outliers and their accumulation across denoising steps are genuine bottlenecks for low-bit quantization of diffusion models, and the motivation is clearly articulated.

The experimental evaluation is broad: LDM-4 on ImageNet, LDM-4/LDM-8 on LSUN-Bedrooms/Churches, and DiT-XL on ImageNet at 256 and 512 resolutions, across W4A4/W4A3/W8A4 and lower-bit settings, with standard metrics (IS, FID, sFID, Precision, Recall).

A component-wise ablation (Table 5) disentangles the contributions of LSQ, LoRA distillation, and the Hadamard transformation, and a dedicated transformation-scheme comparison (Table 6) empirically supports the Single vs. Double Hadamard claim, including latency measurements.
The framework retains the training efficiency of EfficientDM (Fig. 5c), which is a practical advantage over heavier QAT pipelines.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The core method is essentially EfficientDM's LoRA-based distillation with a Hadamard rotation applied to activations only — a combination of two well-established ideas (QuaRot/SpinQuant-style rotations and EfficientDM's QAT recipe). The 'Single vs. Double Hadamard Transformation' distinction is an engineering choice rather than a fundamentally new technique; applying the online rotation to activations while leaving weights in the original basis is close to standard practice in rotation-based PTQ.

Overselling of results in the abstract and introduction. The headline '467.73% IS improvement' at W4A3 is a relative gain over a nearly collapsed baseline (EfficientDM IS 8.74 vs. FP 365); in absolute terms the W4A3 model remains far from usable (FID 33.47 vs. 11.22 for FP). At W4A4, the FID gain over EfficientDM is marginal (6.58 vs. 6.63), despite the claimed 12.8% IS improvement.

The claim that HQ-DM 'outperforms existing methods across these bit configurations' (Sec. 5.2) is not fully supported: at W8A4 on ImageNet, HQ-DM's FID (7.68) and sFID (9.93) are notably worse than EfficientDM (6.75, 8.48). Similar mixed results appear elsewhere; the text does not acknowledge these regressions.

Technical presentation of the convolution path is unclear and possibly unsound. Applying the Hadamard matrix only along the width dimension requires the width to be a (multiple of a) power of two, and the asserted equivalence for strided/multi-kernel convolutions (Eq. 14) is not rigorously justified; the narrative about 'integer-only' convolution is muddled, since a dequantization-like multiplication by Hc appears between quantized activation and the integer convolution, blurring the claimed hardware benefit.

Internal inconsistencies in the ablation: in Table 5, 'Naive QAT + LSQ + Hada.' achieves a better FID (6.47) than the full HQ-DM (6.58), which undercuts the necessity of the LoRA component, yet this is not discussed.

The paper claims 'data-free fine-tuning conditions,' but the method distills from a full-precision teacher fed with xt; the data regime (real vs. synthetic data, how noise inputs are generated) is not clearly specified, weakening both the claim and reproducibility. No code release is mentioned, and many implementation details are deferred to an appendix not available in the manuscript.

The outlier analysis (Figs. 2 and 4) is anecdotal — restricted to a few selected layers and a single timestep — and does not establish that the weight-outlier amplification argument for Double Hadamard generalizes beyond the single examined layer.

Timestep-wise learnable quantization scales multiply the number of scale parameters with the number of denoising steps; the paper does not analyze this parameter overhead or its interaction with sampler step counts (e.g., whether gains hold at fewer DDIM steps, which matters for the efficiency motivation).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: activation outliers and their timestep-dependent behavior are a genuine bottleneck for low-bit diffusion model quantization, and the paper articulates this well.

The Single (activation-only) Hadamard Transformation is a sensible design choice with concrete, well-argued practical benefits: compatibility with INT convolution, and avoidance of outlier amplification in weights (supported by Fig. 4 analysis and Table 6).

Comprehensive experiments across multiple settings: conditional (LDM-4 ImageNet, DiT-XL) and unconditional (LSUN-Bedrooms, LSUN-Churches) generation, multiple bit configurations (down to W4A3/W2A4), and multiple evaluation metrics (IS, FID, sFID, Precision, Recall).

Consistent improvement over the strongest baseline (EfficientDM), with gains growing as activation bit-width decreases, which matches the paper's central claim about outlier sensitivity at low bit-widths.

A thorough ablation study (Table 5) that isolates LSQ, LoRA, and the Hadamard component, plus a direct comparison against the Double Hadamard Transformation variant (Table 6) that substantiates the core design claim, including latency measurements.
Demonstrates scalability to Transformer-based architectures (DiT-XL), which strengthens generality beyond U-Net, and reports training-time costs showing the added overhead is negligible.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the method is essentially EfficientDM's LoRA/LSQ distillation framework (explicitly 'adopted unchanged') combined with an activation-only Hadamard rotation, which is closely related to prior techniques (QuaRot, SmoothQuant, Xi et al.). The contribution is primarily an engineering insight about where not to apply the Hadamard transform rather than a new algorithmic mechanism.

Headline claims are overstated via relative improvements: the '467.73% IS improvement' at W4A3 compares against a baseline that has essentially collapsed (EfficientDM IS of 8.74 vs. FP 365.35). The absolute quality at W4A3 (IS 49.62, Precision 54.87%) remains far from the FP model, so practical utility at ultra-low-bit settings is unproven.

The convolution treatment raises a soundness question: the Hadamard matrix for convolutions is applied only along the last (width) spatial dimension rather than the channel dimension, where activation outliers typically reside. The paper does not analyze or justify why spatial-dimension transformation is effective, which weakens the theoretical grounding of the INT-convolution support claim.

Some experimental comparisons are not fully clean: in Table 6, DHQ-DM conv layers are 'regressed to the Single Hadamard Transformation,' meaning the compared variant is a hybrid rather than a pure Double Hadamard baseline; the claimed 10%+ latency overhead and performance gaps therefore partly conflate implementation and methodological differences.

Latency gains are modest (1.10x-1.14x over DHQ-DM) and absolute hardware efficiency versus the FP model or a real INT kernel is not reported, so the 'hardware-friendly' claim is only partially substantiated.

W4A4 FID results are mixed relative to baselines on ImageNet (HQ-DM 6.58 vs. QuEST 5.98 and Naive QAT+Hada. 6.47 in the ablation), and the paper does not discuss why its best ablation variant underperforms the full model on FID.

Reproducibility is not addressed: no code release is mentioned, and hyperparameter details (LoRA rank, learning rates, number of calibration samples, W4A3 outlier handling choices) are deferred to an appendix not provided.

Writing and presentation issues: Fig. 4's caption is confusingly worded (calling 'Original' a 'Single Hadamard Transformation (no weight transformation)'), the contributions list repeats nearly identical text twice, and the paper lacks an explicit limitations discussion (e.g., dependence on weights remaining low-outlier, applicability to non-power-of-two dimensions beyond the block-diagonal workaround).
